content: The concept of the nadi system in yoga has its roots in ancient texts, with one of the earliest references found in the Chandogya Upanishad. Among the numerous nadis, or energy channels, three are considered the most significant: Ida, Pingala, and Sushumna. The Sushumna nadi is described as the central channel, running along the cerebrospinal axis from the perineum to the top of the skull, where the lambdoid and sagittal sutures meet. Ida, the lunar nadi, is located on the left side of the body, is pale in color, and is associated with negative polarity. Pingala, the solar nadi, is situated on the right side of the body, is red in color, and is linked to positive polarity. While these three nadis are the primary focus, some tantric texts mention the existence of over 72,000 nadis, which originate from the central chakras and extend outward, becoming progressively finer. The Sat-Cakra-Narupana, an early text on nadis and chakras, explicitly describes these three main nadis. It refers to them as Sasi (Ida), Mihira (Pingala), and Susumna (Sushumna). The text poetically describes Sushumna as embodying the three gunas (qualities of nature) and as being associated with the Moon, Sun, and Fire. It is depicted as a string of blooming Dhatura flowers, extending from the Kanda (a subtle energy center near the base of the spine) to the head, with a shining Vajra (a subtle channel) running within it. Nadis are believed to carry prana, the vital life force energy, which is analogous to qi in Chinese systems. Prana, the active energy, is said to flow through Pingala, while apana, the passive energy, flows through Ida. When awakened, kundalini energy is thought to circulate within the Sushumna nadi. Ida and Pingala are often associated with the two hemispheres of the brain. Pingala, the solar and extroverted nadi, corresponds to the right side of the body and the left hemisphere of the brain. Ida, the lunar and introverted nadi, corresponds to the left side of the body and the right hemisphere of the brain. These nadis cross at the optic chiasma, where the pathways of the brain intersect. In addition to their physiological and energetic roles, these nadis are believed to have extrasensory functions, influencing empathic and instinctive responses. Practices such as pranayama, which involves alternate nostril breathing, are thought to stimulate these nadis. For example, breathing through the left nostril is believed to activate Ida and the right hemisphere of the brain, while breathing through the right nostril activates Pingala and the left hemisphere. Such practices are said to purify and enhance the flow of energy through these channels, ultimately aiming to awaken kundalini energy. The term nadi is derived from the Sanskrit root nad, meaning channel, stream, or flow. Rhythmic breathing and specific breathing techniques are believed to influence the flow of energy within these nadis. According to yogic interpretations, these techniques are designed to purify and develop the energetic currents, facilitating the awakening of kundalini energy. In Western esoteric traditions, the three main nadis—Ida, Pingala, and Sushumna—are sometimes compared to the Caduceus of Hermes. The two serpents of the Caduceus are thought to symbolize the kundalini energy or serpent-fire, which moves through these channels. The wings of the Caduceus are interpreted as representing the ability to achieve higher states of consciousness through the activation of this energy. In this mystical framework, the nadis are also associated with alchemical concepts. Pingala is likened to alchemical sulfur, being red, hot, and dry, and is correlated with the Sun. Ida, on the other hand, is compared to alchemical mercury, being cold, wet, and pale like the Moon.
